newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: UK's Blair gets his way on defence.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair gets his way on defence.

text.p: Britain's new Labour Prime Minister, Tony Blair, on Tuesday fought off efforts to give the European Union a defence role, adding to a growing tally of successes at his first formal summit of the bloc.
Flying into Amsterdam, critics from the ousted Conservative party warned that Blair would be "eaten alive" by his more experienced European partners like German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
But emerging briefly from summit talks on Tuesday evening, Blair hailed the deal won after hard bargaining.
"We have reached agreement...which is very satisfying for us because it makes it absolutely clear that our defence interests will continue to be looked at in NATO," said a smiling Blair.

Blair had been refusing to accept plans by other European states, in particular Germany and France, to give the EU a defence role by moving to a merger between the bloc and the Western European Union defence organisation.
Britain argued that a merger would undermine NATO as not all NATO members were in the WEU and that the EU had no track record of successfully coordinating defence or foreign policy.
Other states had tried to get around Britain's objections by suggesting a merger "might in time" take place.

But Blair, arguing it was pointless to agree to anything "in time" if he was opposed to it happening anyway, held firm and -- with the help of non-aligned Sweden and Finland, as well as NATO member Denmark and neutral Ireland -- had the phrase struck out.
In its place, the EU agreed a text saying there was merely a "possibility of the integration" -- a phrase described by British officials as the weakest seen in any pre-summit talks.

Blair's victory on defence came on top of Monday's success in winning agreement for watertight legal protection for Britain's border controls, asylum and immigration policy as the rest of Europe moves to coordinate frontier checks.

Officials also still expect the European Commission to issue a letter promising a tougher approach to quota-hoppers -- foreign, mainly Spanish, fishermen who buy up British quotas but land their catches in other EU states.

So far, Blair has fulfilled the pledges he made before the summit, as well as sticking to the promises of former British prime minister John Major, turfed from office by Labour's May 1 landslide election vitory.

Major, whose defeated Conservatives portrayed Blair as a puppet on Kohl's knee in a now notorious election campaign poster, promised to veto any deal at Amsterdam unless he got a quota-hopping accord and protection for Britain's frontiers.
Blair dismissed suggestions he had had to compromise.

"There is not a single thing that we have yielded up that we said that we would not. So what is very important to recognise is on all the areas; tax, immigration, defence, the British national interest, the British veto is secured," he said.

But Blair -- who also claimed partial credit for Monday's deal on jobs and growth which ended a row between Germany and France and kept preparation for the single currency on track -- contrasted his approach with that of the ousted Major.
Officials said the language of opt-outs and vetos was no longer heard from Blair, who had kept his pledge to put Britain at the heart of Europe without sacrificing Britain's interests.

"We didn't just came here to say let's stop everyone else doing something. We came with the view of putting employment, economic reform, measures on the environment right at the top of the agenda and that we have achieved," Blair said.
"So it's not merely that we have prevented other countries pushing us into things we didn't want to be pushed into. We have, I think, exercised a constructive leadership role."
